name: Maya Chen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Maya, and thanks for your time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or political parties, and everything you say is confidential. Could you start by telling me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: At the moment I'm on a six-storey apartment building made from mass timber, which means big factory-made wall and floor panels of glued layers of wood. A lorry brings the panels, the crane lifts them, and my crew guides them in, screws the brackets, seals the joints and checks everything's level. Before the first lift I've usually photographed the day's drawings and asked an AI app to list the panel order and flag anything that doesn't match the delivery note. It caught a wrong panel two weeks ago, which saved us half a day of the crane standing still.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love how fast it goes up. You come in on Monday to a concrete core and by Friday there's a whole floor of flats you can walk through, and it smells like a sawmill. The hard part is wind, because you can't lift a big flat panel in a gust, so we spend a lot of time standing around waiting, and the boss hates paying for waiting. And my colleague João's English is still patchy, so half my day I'm translating with the phone between us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably say, well, that's a bit of a letdown. I'm the one on site who's always showing people what the apps can do, so the crew would rib me for weeks. Online I'd likely post something like, still useful, just not magic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it'd be fine for me, a little boring. I already get my time savings from checking drawings and translating for João, and if that's as far as it goes, my job stays exactly what it is. I'm not someone who needs the world to change to feel all right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing dramatic. I'd keep using the apps I use, keep my savings ticking over, and maybe look at a course in timber-frame design in a year or two because I like it, not because I'm scared. Dev and I would carry on paying the mortgage the normal way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit flat, like when a film you were excited about turns out average.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the crew would rib you. Who's the loudest?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Big Martin, the crane supervisor. He calls my phone my second brain and asks it daft questions when I'm not looking. He'd have a field day with this one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about this picture you'd actually prefer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably that nobody gets hurt by it. My dad lost a factory job in his fifties and never really got back on his feet, so a world where nothing big shifts has something going for it. I'd just miss the excitement.

S0.say: I'd say it's a bit of a letdown, and the crew would rib me for weeks because I'm always showing off the apps. Online I'd post that it's still useful, just not magic.
S0.think: Privately it would be fine and a little boring, since she already gets real time savings from checking drawings and translating. She doesn't need the world to change to feel all right.
S0.do: Keeps using the AI apps she already relies on and keeps saving as normal. Might take a timber-frame design course in a year or two out of interest rather than fear.
S0.feel: Calm and slightly flat, like an average film after a big build-up.
S0.quote: Big Martin, the crane supervisor. He calls my phone my second brain and asks it daft questions when I'm not looking.
S0.fieldNote: Maya is the site's tech enthusiast and enjoys it; the plateau disappoints her more than it worries her. Her father's job loss in his fifties came up unprompted and seems to sit behind her views. Her daily AI use is very practical and tied to real savings on site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the chance to do it right: retrain people properly, cut hours without cutting pay, and make sure the people doing the work get some of the gain. I'd say that at the union and online, and I'd probably be quite annoying about it. It's not the machines I'm worried about, it's who owns them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd do well out of it. I already speak the language of these tools, and our kind of building is half made in a factory anyway, so I can see my job turning into running the machines and checking their work. What I'd watch is the people around me, like João, who don't have the English or the confidence with screens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my boss straight away to send me on whatever robot or digital training the panel maker offers, and I'd offer to pay half if he said no. I'd keep a list in my phone of every job on site that a machine starts doing, so I know where it's heading. And I'd push the union to set up proper training for people like João, in their own language.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good, mostly. Excited, with a bit of guilt that I'm excited while others are scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where does the guilt come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From my dad, really. He was proud and stubborn and got left behind, and I watched him sit in front of the television for ten years. When I'm cheering about some new gadget, part of me hears him saying, that's fine for you, love.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you help João, practically?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit with him on Thursdays after work and go through the app with him in Portuguese, it does translation fine. And I'd make sure the boss knows he's the best person on site at sealing joints, because a machine might do the screwing, but somebody has to know when the seal's wrong.

S1.say: I'd say this is the chance to do it right: retrain people, cut hours without cutting pay and share the gains with the workers. It's not the machines that worry me, it's who owns them.
S1.think: Privately she thinks she'd do well, since she already knows the tools and timber building is half factory-made. She worries more about colleagues like João who lack English or confidence with screens.
S1.do: Asks her boss for the panel maker's robot and digital training, offering to pay half if refused, and keeps a running list of tasks machines take over. Pushes the union for training in workers' own languages and tutors João weekly.
S1.feel: Excited, with some guilt about feeling excited while others are scared.
S1.quote: When I'm cheering about some new gadget, part of me hears him saying, that's fine for you, love.
S1.fieldNote: Maya's progressive instincts are about ownership and sharing gains rather than resisting change. Her guilt, rooted in her father's experience, gives her enthusiasm an edge of conscience. She moves first and pulls others along, João especially.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is too fast for any government to protect people, so we need emergency measures now: a basic income, a tax on robot owners, rules about notice. I'd say it everywhere, at the union, online, to my representative's office. I wouldn't be pretending it's all fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, this is the one that actually gets to me. My usual plan, learn the tools and run the machines, works for a while, but if the AI can do almost anything, then even the person supervising the robots isn't needed for long. With two years, the politics won't catch up, and that's what scares me, not the technology itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First week, I'd volunteer to run whatever machines our company buys, because being the operator buys me time. We'd stop overpaying the mortgage and build the cash pile instead, we've got a bit over a year saved and I'd want two. I'd spend evenings on the campaign side, writing to my representative and helping the union draft what an emergency deal should look like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd feel in control of my next year, but not of the bigger picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI every day. Does that make this scenario feel different to you than to your workmates?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, because I've seen how fast it's improved in the last couple of years. My workmates think it's science fiction, I think it's next Tuesday. That makes me less shocked, but it also means I can't comfort myself by not believing it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Dev that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, you might be fine for a bit, because parents still want a teacher in the room. Then I'd say, let's sit down Saturday and do the numbers, properly, with a spreadsheet. That's how we deal with things, we make a plan and then we feel better.

S2.say: I'd say this is too fast for any government to protect people, so we need emergency measures like a basic income, a tax on robot owners and notice rules. I'd say it everywhere, without pretending it's fine.
S2.think: Privately this one gets to her, because even supervising robots won't last long if AI can do almost anything. Her fear is that politics won't catch up in two years, more than the technology itself.
S2.do: Volunteers in the first week to operate whatever machines her company buys, to buy time. Stops overpaying the mortgage to grow savings from just over a year toward two, and spends evenings writing to her representative and helping the union draft an emergency deal.
S2.feel: Anxious: in control of the next year, but not of the bigger picture.
S2.quote: My workmates think it's science fiction, I think it's next Tuesday.
S2.fieldNote: Maya's daily AI use cuts both ways: she isn't shocked, but she can't take comfort in disbelief either. Her fear is political, that support systems won't be ready, rather than personal. Her plan is to be the operator first, and she's clear that only buys time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years, which is just enough to build something if we start this winter. Retraining funds, a share of robot profits for workers, and a basic income pilot. I'd say it at the union and in a couple of online groups I'm in about construction tech.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is enough for me to get ahead of it. I've been talking with João and two others about setting up a small crew as a cooperative, a company the workers own, that rents or buys a panel-fixing robot and takes on jobs. If machines are going to do the work, I'd rather we own one than watch the big contractor own them all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, I'd do a proper course in robot operation and site digital management, which I'd pay for myself, maybe two or three thousand. Year two, we'd set up the cooperative and start doing small timber jobs on weekends, garden studios, extensions. By year three or four, if it's working, I'd go part-time at my main job and see if the co-op can stand on its own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a busy, hopeful way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the risk in the co-op idea?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That we buy a machine and the machine is out of date in eighteen months, or that the big firms undercut us. I know that. But I've got enough savings that if it fails, we're not losing the house, and I'd rather fail at that than sit still.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier you said even supervising robots might not last long. Does that apply to the co-op too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, yes, in the end. I don't have an answer for after that, and I don't trust anyone who says they do. What the co-op gives us is a few years of owning something, and a stake when the money's being shared out.

S3.say: I'd say five years is just enough to build something if we start this winter: retraining funds, a share of robot profits for workers and a basic income pilot. I'd say it at the union and in online construction-tech groups.
S3.think: Privately she thinks five years is enough to get ahead, and she'd set up a worker-owned cooperative crew that owns a panel-fixing robot. She'd rather workers own a machine than watch the big contractor own them all.
S3.do: Pays two or three thousand for a course in robot operation and site digital management in year one, then sets up a cooperative with João and two others doing weekend timber jobs in year two. Goes part-time at her main job by year three or four if the co-op works.
S3.quote: If machines are going to do the work, I'd rather we own one than watch the big contractor own them all.
S3.fieldNote: The cooperative idea is where Maya's progressive politics and her appetite for risk meet. She's candid that it may only last a few years and that she has no answer for what comes after. Her savings make failure survivable, which is what lets her try.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is plenty of time to make this good for most people, if we choose to. Share the gains, shorten the week, fund the transition. I'd say it hopefully, for once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years is the version where I think I come out fine. I'd be fifty-three, the co-op could be properly established, the mortgage would be mostly paid, and Dev and I would have time to plan. The question would be the kids, but Ruby and Theo would grow up with this stuff, so they wouldn't be scared of it the way my dad's generation was.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the co-op slowly, maybe year two or three, and grow it while keeping my main job. I'd put some savings into it and some into a pension fund, so we're not betting everything on one thing. And I'd stay involved in the union's tech committee, if there is one, to push for a fair deal on who gets the money from all this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Even a bit excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ruby's eleven. What would you tell her about her future?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her to learn to build things, with her hands and with the computer, and to be the kind of person who asks who owns it. She already helps me in the garage at weekends, she made a bird box last month that's better than mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've been calm here but anxious with two years. What exactly changes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time for the politics, mostly. I trust people to get to a fair deal eventually, it just takes years and arguments. With two years nobody gets that chance, with ten I think we do.

S4.say: I'd say a decade is plenty of time to make this good for most people if we choose to, by sharing gains, shortening the week and funding the transition. I'd say it hopefully, for once.
S4.think: Privately she thinks she comes out fine with ten years: the co-op established, the mortgage mostly paid and time to plan with Dev. She expects her children to grow up comfortable with the technology, unlike her father's generation.
S4.do: Starts the cooperative slowly around year two or three while keeping her main job, splitting savings between the co-op and a pension fund. Stays involved in union tech work to push for a fair share of the gains.
S4.quote: She already helps me in the garage at weekends, she made a bird box last month that's better than mine.
S4.fieldNote: Maya's mood tracks how much time politics has to catch up; she trusts slow democratic bargaining but not fast shocks. She's calm with ten years, which follows from her savings, skills and appetite for change. Her advice to her daughter, to ask who owns it, sums her up.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. I'd personally be all right for a while, but I'd be watching people like João and my dad's old mates go under before anyone in charge has even had a meeting. What would help is emergency rules ready to go before it happens: a basic income people can actually live on, funded by a tax on whoever owns the machines, and free training in people's own languages.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who gets to decide. It always gets talked about like the robots just arrive, like rain. But somebody signs the order for every machine. And I'd like workers to be in the room when that happens, not reading about it in the cabin afterwards.

headlineQuote: It always gets talked about like the robots just arrive, like rain. But somebody signs the order for every machine.
portrait: Maya is a 43-year-old carpenter on a mass-timber apartment building, the site's keenest user of AI apps, which she uses every day to check drawings and translate for a colleague. Her father's job loss in his fifties shapes her progressive focus on who owns the machines. She finds the plateau a letdown and the steady picture an opportunity, but AGI in two years makes her anxious because politics won't have time to catch up. With five or ten years she plans a worker-owned cooperative that runs its own robot, and with a decade she feels calm.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because she'd watch colleagues like João go under before anyone in charge had time to act.
whatWouldHelp: Emergency rules ready in advance: a livable basic income funded by a tax on machine owners, and free training in people's own languages.
